All topics · Indian History · Lesson 4

Indo-Aryans and the Vedic age: what one priestly book can tell us

Two blocks (read ~20 min, lesson ~15 min). One win: judge the claim "caste is unchanged since Vedic times" from the earliest text that mentions it.

Why this lesson

The Indus cities were gone by about 1700 BC. The next people we can name, the Vedic Aryans, left no cities and no inscriptions in India, only hymns their priests memorised. So everything in this lesson rests on one question: what can a book of priestly hymns tell a historian, and what can't it? Caste is the test case, because the oldest description of the four varnas is one of those hymns.

Warm-up: how the Indus civilisation began (5-minute re-teach)

Last lesson, the order of the Indus stages didn't land. Here's why the order matters. The old story said the cities were outposts of Mesopotamia, suddenly planted. The stages are the evidence against that: if the cities grew out of local villages over thousands of years, they weren't planted from outside [1].

Read it as a story of moving downhill and growing: hills → plain → cities → decline. Farmers in the Baluchistan hills (Mehrgarh) came down onto the Indus plain (Amri), the villages grew into planned cities, and at the end people camped in the ruins.

Put these in order, earliest first.

Hills → plain → cities → decline: Mehrgarh (from the 7th millennium BC), Amri (4th millennium), the Mature cities (2600–1700 BC), then Late Harappan squatters. A slow local growth, which is why "an outpost of Mesopotamia" was dropped [1].

Block 1: read first

Reading

Kulke & Rothermund, A History of India, Chapter One, "Immigration and Settlement of the Indo-Aryans":

  1. From the heading "Immigration and Settlement of the Indo-Aryans" through the boxed hymns "Indra, the breaker of forts and donor of wealth" and the paragraphs on the Dasas right after it (about 6 pages). The middle section, "The Vedas as a mirror of historical experience", is the most important part.
  2. Skip ahead to "Social differentiation and the emergence of the caste system" and read it with the box "Primordial sacrifice and the creation of the varnas" (about 3 pages). You can skim "The expansion of Aryan settlements" in between, or skip it.

Notation trap: K&R quote hymns as (Rigveda, X, 90): book X, hymn 90. Book numbers matter in this lesson: books II–VII are the oldest, and books I and X are the latest. A reference with "X" is a late hymn.

Answer the three boxes below as you read, a sentence or two each. They're your notes; every answer gets a reply.

Who composed and passed down the Vedas, and how? What does K&R say that means for using them as a source?

Brahmin priests, by oral transmission "in a most faithful and accurate manner", so the texts are "a fairly reliable source" (well preserved); but they "express the priestly world-view of the Brahmins", so they need critical reading. Credit either half; full for both: reliable as a record of what was said, slanted in whose view it gives.

Who are the Dasas or Dasyus in the hymns, and what's odd about how the hymns treat them?

The indigenous enemies, defending fortified places (purah) that Indra "breaks". Odd: they're disdained, yet chiefs with dasa in their names (Divodasa, Sudasa, Trasadasyu) are praised as allies; Parpola suggests the Dasas were earlier Aryan-related migrants. Credit for noticing the contradiction.

What surprised or confused you in the reading?

No right answer. Reply to it.

Block 2: the lesson

What the Rigveda can tell us (from the reading)

Start from what's solid. K&R put it in two sentences: the Vedic texts, "and in particular the Rigveda, still remain our major source concerning the early phases of Vedic culture", but "these texts express the priestly world-view of the Brahmins" [1]. Both are true at once. Oral transmission kept the words very accurate, so we know what the priests sang. But we only hear the priests.

Can the Rigveda alone answer this, or do we need another kind of source?

The hymns name rivers (the Kubha and Suvastu, today's Kabul and Swat) and call warfare goshati, "getting cattle" [1]. They give only the Aryan priests' side, so the Dasas' view is lost, and they carry no dates: dates have to come from outside the text.

Dating a book that has no dates

If the hymns carry no dates, how does anyone date them? Try it before you look: what kinds of outside evidence could pin down when a text was composed?

Clue 1: a treaty outside India. Around 1380 BC a Mitanni king in upper Mesopotamia signed a treaty with the Hittite king Suppiluliuma I that calls on the Vedic gods Mitra, Varuna, Indra and the Nasatyas [1]. So the gods, and the language of the hymns, already existed by then.

Clue 2: a metal. The later hymns mention iron, and iron came into use in South Asia around 1000 BC. So the latest parts of the Rigveda "cannot be much older than the eleventh century BC" [1].

Clue 3: counting back from the Buddha. Max Müller started from the Buddha (c. 500 BC). The Upanishads come before Buddhist philosophy, the Brahmanas before them, and the hymns before those. That gives about 1200–1000 BC for the hymns. Scholars still mostly accept his chain, with the Rigveda stretched to 1300–1000 BC [1].

Put together: the hymns were composed roughly between the 14th and 11th centuries BC. K&R's chronology calls c. 1400–900 BC the Early Vedic period, and after about 1000 BC, with iron and settled farming in the Ganga–Yamuna Doab, the Late Vedic age [1].

Place the Mitanni treaty that names the Vedic gods (within 60 years).

c. 1380 BC: about three centuries after the Indus cities ended, and the oldest dated evidence of the Vedic gods anywhere [1].

Varna and jati

Two words get translated as "caste", and the claim at the end depends on keeping them apart. Both definitions are K&R's [1]:

  • Varna first meant colour, the badge separating the free Aryans from the subjugated people. It became the name of four broad estates: priests (Brahmin), warriors (Kshatriya), free peasants and traders (Vaishya), and labourers and artisans (Shudra).
  • Jati is the caste one is born into (jata, "born"): the many individual castes. The varnas later served as umbrella categories for them.

The four varnas first appear in one hymn, the Purusha hymn, Rigveda X, 90 [1]:

The Brahman was his mouth, of both arms was the Rajanya [Kshatriya] made. His thighs became the Vaishya, from his feet the Shudra was produced.

What does the hymn's location, book X, tell you about when the fourfold varna order appears in the sources?

Books II–VII are the oldest; book X is late and "contains … evidence of the caste system which is missing in the earlier books" [1]. The early hymns distinguish only ordinary tribesmen (vish), warrior nobles (kshatriya) and priests.

The claim

You'll hear: "Caste is unchanged since Vedic times." Judge it from the reading only.

Using only the reading, say (1) what about caste was already present in the Vedic texts, (2) what came only later, and (3) one reason the Purusha hymn may describe an ideal rather than how society actually worked. Then give your verdict on the claim.

Grades exactly the three named parts (TEACHING-LOG 25), from K&R Ch. 1 only. (1) Present in Vedic times: a ranked order of estates (Brahmin and Kshatriya on top, then Vaishya, then Shudra), stated in the late Purusha hymn; artisans despised as Shudras, and ritual impurity already strong (vessels for the Agnihotra made only by Aryans). Any one. (2) Later: the full jati system, "this full-fledged caste system assumed greater importance only at a much later period"; also the fourfold order itself is absent from the earliest hymns (books II–VII). Either. (3) Ideal vs. reality: the hymns give "the priestly world-view of the Brahmins", and the hymn legitimised the Brahmins' place at the apex: the authors are the ones ranked first. Or: a single late hymn, mythical, not a description. Verdict: false as stated (it changed: from three groups, to four estates, to many jatis), though some ideas (hierarchy, impurity) are very old. Got it = all three parts with no false statement; a reasoned verdict either way is fine.
